WARR INGTON WIREWOIIKERS AT FRODSIIA.M.

The employds of tlo. firm of William Smith and Son. of Hallam Wireworks, Warrington, had a pic- nic, on Saturday, to Frodsham. and advantage was taken of it to make a presentation to the cashier, Mr. Joseph Smith, on the ...mon of his marriage. : The men and other hand. over 18 years of age, to 'the number of 87, left Dallam-lane at half-past ten lin the morning, in a couple of large brakes, sup- plied by Mr. Edward Connor, of Sankey-st., each employe wearing a buttonhole, the gift of kire. Kerr. the wife of the proprietor of the works. On arriving at the Bear's Paw Hotel, Frodslistn,bet ween twelve and one o'clock, the party were met by Mr. and Mrs. Kerr and their family, and Mr. Kite,,. ; who bad it trim from Str. lion about an hour tire- vlollol3'. Bowling on the green attached to the hotel made the time pane pleasantly till dinner was anmunced, shortly after two o'clock. The chair was occupied by Mr. George Smith, and the vi' 'hair by Mr. William Leftwich, and in addition to Mr. and Mrs. Kerr and family, and Mr. Ellison, there were also present Mr. Joseph Smith and his bride, who bad only a few hours previously returned from their honeymoon tour ; Mr. George Clive (ntanager of the works), Mr. Joseph Conner. Mr. Thomas Bayliss, and Mr. Richard Gibson. After an excellent dinner, the Chairman line posed the health of the Queen.—The next toa.st was "The health of the Ono of William Smith and Son," which was given from the chair. Mr. SMoa referred in touching tenns to the late Mr. William Smith, and said he could give way to noose in his admiration of that gentleman, whose energy and forbearance were charm:- teristic. Ile always insisted upon every man doing his duty, and that WWI no doubt one of thermions why the firm had been no prosperous. It was pleasing to see on many old workmen present, which was, in his opinion, a criterion that the masters were gsal and were res- pected. (Applause.) He hoped Mr. Kerr would long be spared to carry on the business, and that the present would act be the last time they would ' have a similar gathering. (liver, hear, and applause.)- -Mr. Kerr, who was received with cheers, suitably re- turned thanks, and remarked that it was a great plea- sure to him to take part in the day's proosslinge ; as well as to respond on behalf of the firm of Wm. Smith and Son. Mr. William Sm)th, sen., was dead, and they mimed the presence of Mr. Janus J. Smith, jun., there wen- still left Mary Ann Smith, Julia Smith, Wm_ Smith, Robert Smith, and MR nile ; and he thought they were repnsentative chips of the old block. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) The Chairman had alluded in gracious terms to the,' manner iu which the late Mr. Smith, son., usedto conduet the husineas of the finn ; Mr. Smith, jun., followed in his step,s ; and he (Mr. Kerr) trusted that he would be able to conduct the; business satisfacto- rily and as efficiently as it had been managed hitherto, and if so he had no fear of the result. (Hear, hear.) He had been connected with them for 15 years, so that he was well acquainted with the previous history of the works, and he could assure them that it would be his endeavour to promote the prosperity of the firm, and that of the men, and also to make them happy and com- fortable. (Cheers.)—Mr. Arthur Baker propued the ' health of the manager, to which Mr. Clive responded.— The Chairman then made the presentation to Mr. Joseph Smith. The presentation took the form of a cruet given by the manager, Mr. (live, and a handsome silver tea and coif.. service, aalwerihrd for by the men. The arrangements for the presentation were made on behalf 'of the ample in by a committee consiet)ng of Mr. George I Smith, Mr. Clive, Mr. Joaepb Cooper, Mr. Thos. Bayliss, and Mr. Richard Gibson. Several valuable presents had been privately made to the cashier previously by Mr. and Mrs. Kerv—lflr. Smith suitably acknowledged the gifts that had been made to him.—Theother toasts weni "The health of ths W..rnmen," " Mrs Kerr and family,- and The visitors." Songs, humoroue and sentimental. were given at intervals by several of the workmen. Miss Kerr created a very favourable impreseion by her singing of •• The little brown jog," and in response to a hearty encore she contributed "The Kerry dance.- The n- mainder of the day was spent ina convivial manner.

Between 500 and 600 men are employed there, and on Monday morning between sin and seven o'clock seven getters entered the cage at the pit mouth to priceed to work. After reaching the bottom of the shaft, it was their duty to have walked down the incline, j but, disregarding the rules, they got into four or live I tubs that were jirocosling to the working. They had , not gone more than a dozen yards h., a hook con- necting the tubs with the chain suddenly gave way, the result being that the tubs dashed at a terrific spend down the incline, which is some 800 or 900 yards in length. One of the men, seeing the danger, jumped out and escapes with some severe cuta and bruises. The others were unable to rescue themselves, and after the tubs had proceeded some distance they left the metals. div.head: RIVAL LOVERS KILL EACH OTHER.
div.p: RIVAL LOVERS KILL EACH OTHER.

IThrove affair of two young men at Mated City, on the border of Idaho territory, United States, has just terminated in a most tragic manner for both of them. , The young men by name Abraham Liken awl Jude Spring, hail located at Malad City last spring, and were in partnership as rancheowners. Roth of the young Men fell desperately in love with the same girl. The affection in each ease was so strong that they could not come to any arrangement as to who should give np his attentions to the object of their devotion. At last there was nothing left, so the young men thought, but to fight a duel for the coveted priZe. Armed with sin shooters, the young men betook thenwelvoi on the 3rd inst. to the brookaide. Several shots were fired, and both own were mortally wounded. The bodies were found n the spot where the duel took place and were Lulu' there. The young lady who woo the cause of the unhappy termination of the young own disappeared Mom the duel took place, and her whereabouts at latest accounts was not known.

div.head: ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE IN
div.p: ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE IN
STAFFORDSHIRE.

A terrible tragedy was enacted on Weilnesday night, at the Comeration Baths, Longton, Staffenlshire. it appears that the baths superintendent, Robed Edward Partner, Farmer, aged 23, had some time aim, resigned his posi- tion, and gave out that he intended going to America with his wife and child. Living with hint at the baths Was his wife's brother,Mbirt Brindley, aged 18. Accord- ing b rumour, his brother-in-law was to travel with him but at seven o'clock on Wednesday night, without any apparent reason, Fanner shot Brindley in the back. Ile used a sit-chamber revolver, and fired four shots at his victim, who, turning round after the first shot, received the others in the front of his body. Jas. Wood, the attendant at tlei Turkish baths, boring the report, I rushed down • but before he had arrived Farmer took poison front a 'bottle which he had in his possession, and quickly fell down in a swoon. The police were imme- diately filched, and three doctors were in prompt atten- dance; but Fanner expimd twenty minutes after the fmrful oceurrence. Feveral times lately he had mid he must ham-ma revolver to take with hint to America, but it is not yet known when or where he obtained the weapon. The injured man Brindley was removed to the North Staffordshire Infirmary, M Stoke-on-Trent. No motive is yet amigned for the rash act. Much sympathy is exile...mil for Farmer's father, who is a prominent man lin the borough, an active member of the Council, and highly respeisted. . .

'Ort'Tbu'rsday,.a coroners jury, at Longton, returned a verdict of suicide whilst temporarily insane in theca,. of Farmer. !kindley, who lies at the North Stafford Infirm- ary in a precarious condition, had not rallied much up . to five o'clock. on Thursday evening.

Ti,. r..arest IC is attything be done to better the r.oodition of the poorest of the T'''' P-"e poor, toil how should we set about it ? 11,i:-: i, :, question, which, we are glad to sheen-v.,. iY Is lug store and inert, considered as the cone,j griov: ride,. Theetatiicienceof the nation is g. item uneasy : and, beyond that, amongst ' those ala t .it on the belief that the object of life 1 is nt.t incrcast. of virtue but increase of riches, there 1 is an lino onfortable feeling that the masses may I Settle day lore.ok in upon their riches, if something is nit deme fee then,. Mr. CII.I3IIIMILLATN ha, ceased tot preccii the dactrine of ransom since be bowl, t tO n,41.-bitu with Betse who toil not neither do they spm : led the doctrine is being preached for :ill that, eel one outcome of it—direct or indirect -is tile I :red strike in London which has lust Is,. terminated by coneession to the demands if the Ids Hirers. There are stone writers who would be thought especially farseeing who have already lagan to make it out that the gain which the men have obtained is Sdnnething illusory: that wages ore after all regulated by the law of supply and demand i Iklei that if an advance is taken by foree. SO to speak, from the capitalist it is impassible that it can lie maintained. It is birth, argued that the unproved pay of the docker will be the means of attracting other Weans-vs, and that in the end—such will be the effect ,tf eampetition - the docker will he in no better position than before. But all this has been said a Inuelret I tittles, and a hundred successful strikes have pr.tved that there is little or nothing in it. Slowly, but surely, the bulk of the labouring classes mat e by isintimions pressure—pressure BO great stn, sometimes reach the "strike" point-- succeeded in increasing their share of the fruits of the bid i and as that increase—small though it be --11 an in the majority of cases become permanent. the result is a refutation of the theory that labour tiontlicts are of no service in raising the standard of wag. s. Better payment invariably means a higher stateliesti et living, and, as that standard become in tine• what rimy 'to called a fixture, it means that the partitmlar dass of workers which has secured an advance has secured aa improvsment which will reptant with them. It is quite true that as ~no body of werknum gets it. increase of pay there is oampetition lima the hoditst of workmen below to share tine increase i and it is in this way, as it seems to, its, that the hope lies of permanently bettering the condition al the poorest of the poor.

The succiss of the dock hammers, printers labourers, tailors, &e., loves the way for the bet- ter pynclit of the worst imid toilers in the aomitry. It is a matter mainly of organization, oubesion. and material support. Unfortunately, I the lower the strata, the less likelihood there 111111011 a these fititors into operation. Where linwt help is needed, there is as in rule least given, and that is why the weak mid the poor are oppri-sed all the world over. Still all hope is not exelmled. Who would 'nave predated twin months ago that the dock labourers if the metropolis would strike work as one man, would hold to- gether as One man, would excite the admiration and sympathy of the world by the display of a patient. law-abiding spirit, thereby gaining the greatiat battle that Labour has yet WOll ill its strieigle with Capital 1 What is medial now is that the revolution which has begun shall go lower and hover, until there is better pay for those who are banished to the slums of our large cities--for those who work, work, work and starve whilst they work. We shall be told by the bard- shell political is,inoinist that such ideas are impracticable and I "topian ;but the same political economist would never reckon on Sentiment as a factor, and, as conseqvumee, he would never have been able to pericive that Sentiment would bring the 111 whers scores if thousands of pounds--that it would hi fact prove tin lo thelllucher striking in at the right moment to enable General ltrnxs tin WilllilaWaterloo. As several classes of labourers have sueceeded, why ithinuld it sent be poasible, with similar imeans, for all the climes below them to succeed !' %Would it undermine the founda- thaw of the world if midiih-Inakors had something , mon, than two pnimso a gross 1. Or would ty " collapse if those who imake frilled tennis aprons were paid something more than live pence diizim Oh. if workers of this class, and a score of oth, classes, iambi only strike, and strike effectually, receiving support as the dockers have received somiort, what a glori ~,, s thing it would be 1 What an uplifting id the poorest of the poor !
And who shall ;:ty that it eiun;ot he done
invite our millers tip diwuss this lalamr problem. We have touched hut a corner of it. and shall Moro t. it again.

AT an inquiry which was held at Swimming. Runcorn, on Tuesday, into the cir- cumstances of the death of a girl of fourteen, who had been donvimd in the canal in the presence if ieveral of her companions, sonic pertinent remarks were made on the desirability of boys and girls being taught to swim. Mr. W. HASKINSON, the foreman of the jury, said many lives had been lost in Runcorn through the inabi- lity of the victims to swim a few yards. Runconi certainly stands in especial need of public baths, for it is a maritime town, and it is a matter of course to say that the inhabitants run more risk of des g than those who dwell inland. It is the expense that blocks the way, but if there is no person sufficiently wealthy and sufficiently philanthropic to adopt the Coroner's suggestion, the Commissioners ought to take it upon themselves to build baths at the cost of the town. Apart from the question of swimming, cleanliness is worth something, for, as the poet THOMPSON tells us— Even from the body's purity the mind Receives a secret sympathetic aid. Cleanliness indeed is said to be nest to godliness; but this scarcely holds good of Runcorn, for there are plenty of churches and chapels, but no baths. With regard to teachieg the young idea how to swim, the Coroner remarked that it would be more useful than a groat deal they did teach in Board Schools. We quite agree with him, though why he singled out Board Schools we are at a loss to understand, as the remark applies with equal force to all elementary schools. In the good time com- ing, we shall have Free Education, and, perhaps, Free Baths, while if baths are free, learning to swim, like attendance at school, will be compulsory.

The Bishop of Manchester strikes a Protestant note when he says he does not approve of the proposal to establish an order of Church of Eng- land Monks. Preaching at New Bury, he pro- ceeded to show, what emits very little showing, that wealth does not necessarily mean happiness. "humming personal. he said:—' The happiness of ! his heart dependusl on Ws: Thad in Christ he had !obtained that peace of mind which passes all understanding. which was equally given to the richest and poorest." There is something hi this: but there are men who are huressed with debts and dims who believe they would have peace of mind, tim, if, like Dr. Moorhonse. they were assured of an immune of over £3,000 a year.

Now is the world growing honest. The Bishop of St. Asaph has also been speaking out. On Mon- day his lordship pr3sided over the opening meeting of the annual Diocesan Conference, held ut Rhyl Town Ball, 31111, referring to the titha, agita tins, he said "it was the duty of the clergy to show that they were more anxious to earn than to receive tithes." Gmal, and yet again good. This is the sort of talk to set people thinking. If St. Asaph will kindly encourage them, they will begin to wonder how it happens that for serving the Lord he gets £1,200 a year, and the Archbishop of Canterbury as much as elti.ooo a year. Can they be said to "earn" these large salaries?

A few days ago Signor Crispi, the Italian Premier, was struck with a stone whilst he Was driving out with his daughter. The prisoner's ex- planation of the assault is that he had had nothing to eat for two days' and he was desperate at see- ing the Pre:oier and his daughter looking so con- tented. The explanation is intelligible. We are !acquainted with a workman who relates that. I stranded in New York, and reduced to his last dollar, he was in a despairing state of mind, when, I passing a well-lighted room, the tune of " H sweet home " burst on his ears. This no maddened I him for the moment that he threw n stone through the window. Then he harried away, feeling that he had done a desperate and foolish thing.

conclusion which the narrative does not warrant—that the rich must go to hell and the poor go to heaven. This is a distorted application of the parable. If I read aright, tlw inference I draw is that Dives was a rich man who neglected the duties which-wealth entails. A anall poi.- thin of that wealth would have made Lazarus compara- tively comfortable ;it would have given him wholesome and nourishing food, decent lodgings, and proper sur- gical attendance ; bettet than the dogs coold give. It shows too that the brote was better than the man ; he was a selfish, self-indulgent man--quite unfit for the society of pure beings in another world Lazarus did not gain heaven because he NMI poor—but because he ! lived a pure life. Reading between linen, we find that : Dives neglected the social and moral diniwi which we ' may fairly assoine that Lazarus observed. They had MOSPA and the prophets" which the one observed, the other did not. Mr. Peers calls CountTolstoi an impractical enthusiast, and `• a religious fanatic." Let him be either, he is doing what be can to Icoson the sum of human misery, and for that he &sena% the respect and approval of all good men. Let hint do it in his own way. Fanaticism arid enthusiasm seldom follow the Tolstoi lines. Mr. Peers attributes our -National poverty to " over- production," and the remedy, or one of the remedies, a ri,triction tqwn marriage and a forcible seizure of the income of the married, at the rate of so much per child. His method would be an incentive to crime—to baby- farming, drug dosing, immorality, and child murder. A substantial bakince at the bankers may, or may not, he a dimity sin. If acquired by honest thrift and industry, it inay be a blessing ; but if obtained by fraud, by dis- [ honesty, or by oppreAsing the poor it may be acurse. MR. JOHN PEERS ON MALTHUS AND OVER- PRODECHON.

read the letter of Mr. John Peers, in last week's ! " Examiner." with a great deal of intert-st, but I most I say that I totally disagree with the views he sets forth in the last paragraph. Alluding to the poverty of the I dock labourers, he says," probably the ancestors of these I men may hayi: inobbed Malthus. Had they but profited I by putting into practice his bsiching, everybody would have been the better for it." It is surprising to me that anyls sly can mit forward the doctrine of Malthus as an explanation tot' the poverty which prevails in England at I the present tittle. What was it that !Malthus taught ? That there w-iis a constant tendency °lithe part of the population to outgrow the inetins of sulisience—or, to put it in the definite language of :Malthus himself, that populatio : grew at a geometrical rate while, the produc- tion of fatal could only be increased at an arithmetical rate. Now what are the facts of the last fifty years ? Exactly contrary to what Nlalthus taught. Instead of pnpulatitffi growing at a more rapid rate than the means I of subsistent, .we first that during the reign of the Queen the increase of wealth hat beell three times greater than that of populatian. In the face of this one fact can Mr. Peersargue that an excessive gn:wth tif population Is the cause of the disgraceful amount of poverty which exists in England to-day? "lath mysitt, aeatnco4te,Mr Peers, "what to the main cause of these troubles ? And the answer eomes plain and unhesitatingly—oyer production : tho harvest is plentiful but the labourers are superabundant." If Mr. Porn will allow me to toll him. his two explanations contradict eaeli other. With Malthus he says that there are more rnoutip brought into the world than can to. fed, and then, setting up as a theorist himself, he says there is " over-proshirtion- of the very things which are required to feed anti to clothe people and to make them comfortable. For over-produetittn is a relative term. It means that there are mare articles or commodities pro- duced than can be consumed. To put it another way, Mr. Peer's theory of over-production amounts to this, that people are hungry because more food is produced than can be eaten, that they are ragged and poorly clad because ton touch tit tth is manufactored, and that they are bare-font'ff because there are too many shoes. 7 confess I cannot fathom Mr. Peers' moaning when lie says, " the harvest is plentiful but the labourers are superabundant " If that means anything it must mean " under-production," anti not " oyer-produetion," for no matter how " plentiful" the harvest inay be in itself, if it is not sufficient to meet the requirements of those dependent upon it, it is a case of under-production. I am in hopes that, after Mr. Peers has given a little more consideration to this part of the subject of his letter, he will throw his able pen on the side of those " pseudo-stilt iinental" persons who hold that the poverty and hardships, which so large a proportion of the people of this count ry have to endure, are due neither to over- population oar to over-production, but to the unjust and unequal distribiltion of national wraith, and who hold, further, that there are many ways, by private effort anti combination and by public legislation, in which the injustice and inequality- of this distribution may be redressed.—Yoors, Warrington, Sept. 17, 1889.

div.p: THEOSOPHIC DOGMAS.

Sir,—With your permission, I should like to express my gratification at the interesting condition of your cor- respondence columns, and also give vent to a few opinions on the matter of Theosophy. Mr. Coryn has been rather busy of late, probably owing to the promin- ence given to the Society, of which he is so energetic a fellow, by the accession of Mrs. Besant. Without going into the alleged exposure of the high priestess of the movement, Madame Illavatsky, I wish to calmly and dispassionately disouss the question on its merits. But I am afraid that our western logic will experience scant courtesy when confronted by the wild imaginings of the eastern mystics. However, that remains to be seen. What moreconcerns us is that this bashed-up Buddhism is offered to us as the religion of the future—as the true light to chase away the gross material darkness of the nineteenth century. ! We are told that. "Theosophy attaches no efficacy to , I any creed whatever,' and, further," no creed is required . lof ;he Them-moist." One would infer from this that creeds are of no importance, and that Theosophy is without a creed. But this Wollia hardly be the troth. Thessophy has a erred, for how ean we otherwise know it Into env other 'osophy and if creels are inefficaulons why then trouble to spread the 11,111:IA of Theosophy? The important teachings "of which Mr. Carve writes, what are they but his creed ? And what is his letter hot evidence of the importance he attaches to those teach- ings ? It is the fa.shion to decry creeds. Theshnpler and emnprehensive they are. the better for the peace of Christendom ; but as for becoming creedless, that fan only happen when we are so unfortunate as to become brainless.

Mr. Coryn's creed is certainly more mystical than simple, and contains a larger number of articles than I imagine he will care to admit. It will conduce to clear- ness it! tabulate them. The following are drawn ex- clusively from Ida letter in last week's " Examiner",— I. There is an all-embracing Divine. 11. The spir"
11. The spirit of man is a (Erect emanation from the
111. This " emanation" heroines a pers.. IV. That this person is destined to again become im- personal and to re-nnite with the Divine. . . .

.... . V. That personality may lx, destroyed by persistent altruism, i.e.. self-sacrificr, mid by no other means. VI. That man has more than enable onthis earth. VII. That, in fact, he only attains peace after he has lived many lives 'narked by earnest effort at self-annihi- lation.
—VIII. That this dogma of Re-inearnation is the only one that even atteinpts the solution of the awful pro- bloat of human W."

IX. That there are such things as sesownees " of deeds. Ali thew dogmas are contained M Mr. Coryn's short letter, and I expect there are mom to follow. If he is prepared to urge their reasonableness, I shall be glad, sir, with your consiht,to examine his proofs. And now a few words in conelusion. Does Theosophy I offer anything new ? If no, what? Is Theosophy suited Ito the wants and aspirations of the masses engaged in the toil and bustle of life? As for the principal object of the society, is. "The formation of the nucleus of an universal brotherhood of lunnanity," Theosophy is nineteen eenturies late in the field, and even now appears in borrowed garments. In the ages past the Peasant King of Nazareth, with weary hands and burdened heart, laid the foundations of the kingdom of man, on the adamantine principles of eternal righteousness. Ma; for poor Theosophy.—Souts truly, W. IL BUTLER. I Latchford.

Sin—Under the above heading Mr. John Peen favours yourreademinyour last issue, with an interpretation of the parable of our Lonl,the originality of which no thought- ful man will care to dispute. Its correctness is another thing; and I claim your permission to put side by side with Mr.reers's reading another, and, I venture to think, a better and more accurate one.

In the first place, Mr. Peers is singularly careless in his I dealing with the setting of the great truth which Christ wished to make clear. Here we have," he says, the rich man sent to hell and the poor man sent to heaven?' If Mr. Peers will consult the Revised Version, he will find that there is no such contrast in the destination of the two as is implied in his bald statement, bald, and ontrue As well, inasmuch as it conjures up before the minds of your readers the sensuous scenes of a popular, but onseriptural, heaven, and the horrors of a popular, but equally unscriptural, hell. It is, however, with Mr. Peers's interpretation al the main lesson rif the parable find most fault. He says" Do have the rich man sent to hell and the paorman to heaven. And why ? Because the one term mit end the othor mo. poor, [The italics are I mine.] In the absence of any other reason, we must I accept this very poor one as being, in the opinion of the founder of Christianity. an adeqoate one for the condemnation of one man to eternal torment, and elevation of tlui other to the regions of eternal bliss." . Mr. Peers'a deductions from this unfounded premise are logical enough, but flippant and foolish in the light al a correct understanding of the parable. In seeking to explain the truth hem proclaimed by Christ. I shall notjtake refuge in " original text "and learned comments. I shall simply give he impression produced. on what Mr. Matthew Arnold calls a plain man," in reading the text of the Revised Version. Christ presents ns with a drama in two acts. In the first we ' are introduced to the rich man will fares somptuously every day, and is attired in purple and fine linen. :lath- ing is Add in condemnation of either the feeding or the " attire ; there is no evil in grusl friml or in gond clothes RA Ruch. But outside the open window of Dives the ' beggar sits and watches the feast. Fergood food he has the contemptuously thrown crionlo for clothing, rags. Now it is in the relations of these two characters, that the plot of the drama consists. What will hethe effect on each? The future of Dives depends on his treatment of ; Lazarus and,likewise, that of Lasarus on his bearing to- . wards Dives. Thespectator, in gauging their respective fixtures, can only find assistance in the hints given in the eharacterizatiou. Dives apparently contents himself j with allowing (perhaps ignorantly), the crumtts to be given to Lazar.. He procures him no physician to heal his sores ;he lacks the pity of the very dogs. Then comes the climax of the drama in the death, first, of !I Lazarus. then of Dives. . .

The sewaid act preeents to aotho two men in a pet- , mortal state. The forces at work in the character of each during his lifetime have driven them far apart, a great gulf is fixed over which neither may paw. The beggar ha. f I band rest. whilst the rich man li tormented. And what were those forces ? Christ had Pharisees in his audience. To them the parable was addressed. div.head: BEER BOTTLES AND BOTTOM LOCKS.
div.p: BEER BOTTLES AND BOTTOM LOCKS.

Sir,—The remperance question is to the front now-a-1 days, and Mr. Hardy was at Runcorn lecturing a few I days ago, and informed his hearers in Devonshire 1 agUate that £4OO per week less were spent in drink in Widnes since the establishment of the Lnagueof the Cross I in that locality. Every pia& where a large number of men were employed had his attention except BottOtu Locks. Probably fear are acquainted properly with the fact that hundreds of pound., are spent in drink down Bottom Locks every week ; and. on inquiring, I find that those in authority are not acquainted with it either, although there are gaffers who allow the men to spend and drink away their hard earned money in such a way. The men work "piece-work," as a rule, and several times during the day an emissary is sent out of thegang , to" fetch the beer . It is generally brought to the place . of work in a jar enclosed in a bag in order to deceive anyone who nmy suspect them. Weights are carried in like manner from place to place at the docks, and it is in this way that a man is tempted to have his share out of the bottle, and when Saturday conies he htts to pay his share out of his weekly wages, or, if he does not pay the next week, it is sure to be stopped out of his pay by the second gaffer at the gang, who always draws the money from the office. This kind of thing has been going on for years, arid it is time it was put a stop to. I know one in authority whn used formerly to give notes for al- lowance at his favourite "pub." but now he gives money instead. Neyertheless,the beer is brought down in bottles to the works just the same. I fully believe that if this kind of drinking at work was put a stop to, the men would not have to pay half their wages on the Saturday, and the wives and families wmild not have 101 w going to the publichou., where he is paid Ids wages, and hauling lam out becauae ht. is afraid to go home with little wages. If one in a gang is resolute, and does not send for his bottle in turn, lie is looked upon ass " blackleg," .ven if he is a pledged teetotaller. The only way, in my opinion, is to put a heavy fine on any man found bringing intoxirating drink on the job, or dismiss Win altogether. li-all upon those who regsrd the welfare of the work- men at the docks to inquire into the above statement themselves. and Hies will find it correct. I appeal to every man of philanthropic prineffilea to assist and identify themselves with this movement. It should embraCe livery oilier man ass fellow worker in the same field, wholes:he be pledged or not. There are senora] a...D.1s intender] to promote sobriety and the spread of temperance in Runcorn, and this should he one of the duties they could undertake, thereby bringing peace and happiness to many a home', because if the father of a family does tint drink it in this manner during the week, it would be 'impossible for him to spend it all on a Sat...day, anti so nitieli more would he left for bread and beef. I will write more about this, and endeavour to remedy this deplorable state of things. I ascribe to this its.. a deal of the horrible degradation existing amongst our people at Runcorn. When iny ohjoet is carried, it will be a glad d.tv, not only for fathers and mothers, but for the poor Mae defenceless children who cannot plead for themselves, who present ouch a sight in our streets as to touch the hearts of every Irian that is—l will not say Christian—but even that is humane. Apologising for trespassing on your valuable spare. I remain, sir, youffi, ALPHA.

div.head: WORKS OF COUNT TOLSTOI
div.p: THE WORKS OF COUNT TOLSTOI

ISir,—So my friend, Mr. Peers, has funned an opinion of Tolstoi the very opposite of my own. Ilk letter, in your issue of Saturday last, caine rather as a surprise to me. His impression of Tolstoi is that he is" an Unprac- tical enthusiast, or what COUlee to the sante thing, a religious fanatic, or what some people would pre- fer to call, a thorough-going and zealous Christiae." Ile further takes exception to Tolstoi on the ground that he advocates the carrying out of the doctrines of Christ literally and entirely," and he goes on to say that because we are told to" Resist not evil that therefore "there is an entire and insurinouutable antagonism between the doctrines of Christianity and what is regarded as the solid foundation of civilized society." Certainly, there are doctrines in the Dospels which would prove very difficult of application—but that would not, with Tolstoi, be any reason for their not being applied or carried into practice. I think I suffi- ciently indicated in my previous letter that Tolstoi, whilst accepting and carrying into practi. the teachings of Jesus, is °pissed to many of the dogmas and formulas of the various churches. So that, whilst accepting the 1 teachings of Jest,. in a strict sense, he enjoins own all the absolute nereasity of being guided by reason. But Mr. Peers goes beyond Count Tolstoi altogether. He thinks " Christianity " is "out of touch with the rational basis of modern society "and, that, by" carrying out its precepts literally anti entirelywe sh -add tend to re- vert to the impracticable, fanatic asceticism of the dark ages and modern society would lose whalthey rightly take to be one of their peculiar blessings—the fruits of Ike use of right reasiming—stearn, electricity, Re." I hope my friend, Mr. Ners,won't be annoyed if I charac- terise all this as utter bosh, sheer twaddle. I know these are not elegant or polite terms to apply to any one, muck less to one whom I nape., and am pleased to call my friend. But Mr. Peers's assumptions:are altogether too gratuitous and too far-fetched. And ha instances the story of Dives and Lazarus, and asserts that Dives WWI sent to hell because he was rich, and Lazarus was sent to heaven because he was poor. 'Now Mr. Peers must know very well that Jesus never intendisl to con- vey any such impression. Such au idea. I feel sure, would not occur to one person in a thousand. It cer- tainly never occurred to me, and, before reading Mr. Peers's letter, I never heard of anyone drawing such an inference from the story. tam altogether at issue with Mr. Peers, onto the ' effect of Christianity upon our modern civilization. So 1 far from being effete, or impracticable, I ant convinced I that were its teachings more literally interpreted, and 1 niore honestly and universally carried into practice, I this world would hen much more desirable place to live 1 in than it is. "The wilderness" would, indeed," blossom ! like the rose." Suppose such a state of things to exist as a general acceptance and practice of the teachings of I Christ. We should have no ware. Legions would not , contend against legions—fire and ;sworn, carnage and ' destruction, and all the horrors Cl sanguinary conflict I I would be no more. There would be no inurderers, no I liars, no slanderers, no thieves, no drunkards. The lieensing laws would be von est. We should have an Ideal Commonwealth, besides which those of Moore and I Bacon and of Campanello,are not to he mentioned. Anti there would, certainly, be less running after " filthy lucre.- Christ has condemned covetousness and love I of itches. its have Horace, and Marcus Aurelius, and Epietetus, and Seneca, and Emerson, and Ruskin, and Tolstoi. Instead of the cruel doctrine of the weak going to the wall,we should have a far-reaching,brotherly love, an I all-pervading humanity, which WOUhl feell the hungry, 1 anti help the distressed, and bind up the wounds of the 1 broken-hearted. If everybody laid hold of these teaeli- 1 ; bogs we should have no idle and improvident people I amongst us. . .

And ao to a man hoarding up riches angl living a life of luxury and self-gratification whilst there are starving poor around him—why, we needn't go to Christ, nor yet ti Tolstoi to be told that this is a sin. John Ruskin sano! that no nation has a right to indulge in luxuries mail all its poor are comfortably housed and fed." I hope your readers, and Mr. Peers, will not mistake me. lam very far, indeed, from bring soundly orthodox. Whilst believing in the teachings of Christ, I am de- cidedly of opinion that, in the course of cen- turies, religion has becoene encrusted and defaced by false philosophieo and absurd and illogical dogmas. But is religion, therefore, to be east aside as being of. no use Is the diamond to be despised because it lien 'rat- bedded in clay 1 Tolstoi is not orthordox. He will have nothing to do with the dogenas of the Fagot original sin, and of eternal punishment, and various other dogmas tie , eipially discards. But he says with Clirist—" He that bath two coats, let him impart to him that hath none ; and lie that bath meat, let him do likewise." He believes in the golden rule of doing to others as he would like ethers ,to do unto him. He is more concerned about Lazarus Icing decently fed, and clothed, and housed, than about Hives going to hell. He rises above all the pettiness, awl , jealousy, and bitterness of sectarianism. and mounts to I a higher altitude Wed a Purer atmosphere— ' Like some tall cliff that lifts its nonfat form, . .
Swells from the vale and midway hraveVtn;.;torin.

div.head: JOHN GANDY.
div.p: JOHN GANDY.
WHIPPING A HORSE TILL IT JUMPS INTO A CANAL.

Two boatmen, living at Lymm, named John Gumt and John Banner, were charged at Lymm Sessions, yester- day, with cruelly ill-treating a horse on the 24th August. A policeman—P.C. Cook—said that he saw the horsepull- lug cone boats along the Bridgewater Canal near Broom- edge. Guest jumped off the boat and began whipping the animal in a very violent manner, and after he went on to the boat again, Banner got off and kept up the flogging till the horse, to escape the whip, jumped into the water. It was pulled out with chains and then seemed thoroughly exhauster Lits nostrels projecting, out, and its skin perspiring very much. Guest produced a whip which he arid he had beers using, and Mr. Lister, one of the inagistrates, said it was a pity the defendants could not have it laid over their own backs. A fine of 10s. 13d.end costs,l2.s., was imposed in each case, the bench intimating that if another case of the kind came before them a fine of £2 would be inflicted.

div.head: MARRIAGE AT HALEBANK.
div.p: MARRIAGE AT HALEBANK.

On Wednesday morning a marriage, in which much local interest was taken, was celebrated at Hale Church, in the presence of a numerous coa- -1 gregation when Mr. Andrew Gardiner, youngest son of the late Mr. John Gardiner, of Halebank, was united in the bonds of matrimony with than Martha Daintith, youngest daughter of Mr. William • Daintith, wire and brush maker, Ilalebank. The Rev.. R. Stewart Vicar of Hale, was the officiating clergyman. The bride wino was given away by • her father, wore a white GGltmere dress trimmod with white moire silk, with bat to match, and carried a beautiful humplet. The bridesmaids were Miss Rodgers and MiAs Gardiner of Ilalebauk, and Miss Dain- tith of Warrington. and they wore dresses of cream cash- mere with hats to match. Mr. Joseph Daintith, of War- rington, discharged the duties of best man, and ID. Robert Gardiner and Mr. John Jackson (Widnes were groomsmen. After the ceremony breakfast was provided at Mr. Dkintith's and later the bride and bridegroom left tor Bannotith, where they are spending the honeymoon. The bride's travelling dress was made of silver grey cash- mere. The happy couple received numerous t.ostly presents.

div.head: TERRIBLE ACCIDENT NEAR ?RODMAN'.
div.p: TERRIBLE ACCIDENT NEAR ?RODMAN'.

Henry Sutton, 18 years 01 age, fireman, met his death On the Fnalsham section of the Ship Canal, f,n Monday aftentoon, under terrible circumstances. Deceased and two others were engaged on an engine drawing some 12 or 14 heavily laden wagons At a certain junction the pants, it lactated, had not been accurately adjusted, and the locomotive went off the metals. anticinating danger denased jumped off the engine, falling upon his head. He stumbled under the wheeta, one of which passed ones his head, killing hits instantaneously. The unfortunate youth would in all probability have been quite safe had he not junn,ed off the locomotive. The driver and mother attendant who stuck to their posts on the engine Well` not in any way Injured. On Thursday his remains were interred in the churchyard of the Prod- -boos Parish Mitch, in the presence of nearly a thou- s old friends. After a hymn had been sung by the Mission Choir and a touching address by Mr. Dennis, of the Catnd Works Mission, in which he, in a few sympa- thetic words, referred to the high tone of the deceaseds' character, and impressed upon all who were present the great necessity of making preparation for the life to , come, the funeral eartOr left the home of the deceased [ shortly before four o'clock, his remains being home by r eight fellow-workmen, followed by the cleceaseds I parents, relatives, friends, undo long, procession of work- men connected wins the works, who wen, anxious to pay , their last token of respect to the deceased. div.head: DURHAM TRAGEDY.
div.p: A DURHAM TRAGEDY.

A man named William Walker is supposed to have poisoned hi, wife, and then committed suicide, at Fence- , houses, Houghton-le-Spring, on Thursday morning. Walker, after depositing the dead bod.y of his wife on the bed in the front room of their house, went not, having, ; previousW told his children that ho believed their mother o was dead. The man was afterwards seen on the railway near the Margaret Pit, and shortly after bin body with the head nearly severed, was found not far front where ' first seen. A train of thirteen wagons passed over lois neck. Inspectpr Cruikshanks, Sergeant Fawcett, and Pudney were soon on the spot. Dr. Loraine was ' called in to see tile bodies, and pronounced both dead. lAt the inquest, on Friday, on the victims of the dolphin tragedy, Durham, it was found that the woman Walker had died ofroni suffocation, and that her husband ' had committed suicide.

div.p: Ara:METED WIFE MURDER.
.• ......... At the OldiTail;n7:o7n—Friday, Leonard Howes Fiend- ford, was sentenced to 14 years' penal servitude for shooting his wife with intent to murder.
A.YOTHER.DEATII FROM. HYDROPHOBIA.
A girl named Frances Marian Smith from Lower Tooting, died yesterday morning. at St. Thomas Hospital, London, from hydrophobia. Her father and brother were bitten by the same dog.
THE TAILORS DISPUTE.

A large meeting of delegates from the London branches of the Atnalgatnated Society of Tailors, was held on . Thursday evening, to consider the East-end tailor's , strike. It was revolved that the Executive Collrleil ob- I Min not le. than £lOO to assist the East-awl strikers. DECAPITATED ON THE. RAILWAY.

Yeiterday morning the mutilated body of a man was found on the London, Chatham, awl Dover Railway, near Lordship Lane station, on the Crystal Palate line. On wand] being made the head was afterwards found fifty yards away. The body has not yet been identified.

div.head: DUNDEE EI.EC CION
div.p: DUNDEE EI.EC CION

The writ for the election:4a member of Parliament for Dundee to fill the vaoancy caused by the death of Mr. J. F. B. Firth, wua received at the eity on Friday. The returning officer has fixed Wednesday next for the nomi- nation. It is believed that Mr. John Long, tiladstonian candid:de, will not be opposed.

THE ELECTRIC LIGHT AT BRADFORD. At Bradford on Friday morning' the first electrie ' station established by an English Corporation was opened. The continuous current system hus been adopted, inasmuch as it is contemplated in the near future to utilize the installation for motive power as well as lighting. The price charged by the Corporation at present is about double the price of gas._ _

div.head: LIVERPOOL .CANACSCREME.
div.p: LIVERPOOL .CANACSCREME.

At the hall-yearly meeting on Friday, of the Leeds and Liverpool Canal Company, in Liverpool, it was n.solveil that Parliamentary powers I,- sought for the improvement of the canal scheme, which included the deepening of 103 miles of the canal to Oft. Bin., so that flats carrying 80 tons can use it. The erecting of ; reservoirs and the construction of large lx,rges, at an estimated outlay of nearly a million sterling, is a part of !the scheme. The improvement is expected to increase the traffic and nine working expenses.

div.head: IDENTITY OF" JACK THE RIPPER."
div.p: THE IDENTITY OF" JACK THE RIPPER."

New York Herald" of -yesterday, ref;:ring to Dr. Winslow'o discliworeo,says i—Furtherinterviews have , taken place, and additional material come to hand. It is believed that "Jack the Hipper" has an accomplice, I and that the murders take place M some cases a day, in others two days, before the mutilated bodies are found by the police. This view has limit held all along by the gentlemen who are on the track of the prime author of the Whitechapel initialers, and the Backchurch-lane cowry converts the sumicim into a i7ertainty. The gentlenain who are now interesting themwlves in the case are procisiding upon no shadowy theory, but upon material, substantial, and well authenticated facto.

div.head: SIIOCHINO FATALITY ON THE _HIGHWAY
div.p: SIIOCHINO FATALITY ON THE _HIGHWAY

A profound sensation was caused in Leamington, yesterday morning, by the information that a murder had been committed on the highway, between Radford and Offithurch. It appears that at an early hour on Friday morning, the police found the body of a middle- ' aged man, lying on the roadway quite dead, with either a bullet shot or stab in the body. No weapon was any- where near the body, showing that it was not a case of suicide. A shepherd dog was watching faithfully over the laxly, and refused to be driven away. Tha police at once removed the body to the nearest public-house, and are pursuing inquiries throughout the district The victim turns out to be a Leamington poacher named Brookes. Ile was poaching on Lord Aylesford's °tate, when a fanner named Russell stumbled over one of his rabbit nets and broke it. An altercation ensued, and Rwtsell shot the man in the abdomen, the bullet passing through the body.

At the Old Bailey, on Thursday, George and Agnes Dale, man and wife, were sentenced to ten and five , years' penal servitude respectively for practising illegal operations on women. There were seven indictments, I to all of which prisoners pleaded guilty. I The Lancashire and Yorkshire Association Of Raptist Churches held a conference On Wednesday at Halifax. At the afternoon session a paper on "Recreation in relation to the spiritual life of the churches" was din- cussed, in the isturse of which speakers pointed to I various evils surrounding the games of football and I cricket.

—AC:C.-Writing to a Rome telegram, a new slave trade convention has just been signed on behalf of their • ressective Governments by Lord Salisbury and Signor Catalani, the Italian Minister in London. The provisions I of the Convention are of a more stringent nature than ! those of any other slave trade convention hitherto I concluded. . .

M.P., who form part of the deputation of English Liberals now In Ireland.
